column3: It exactly pairs setting another god beside Allah with severe punishment.

It supplies a broad background of Allah alone giving guidance or leaving astray.
It closely repeats the ban on calling another god with Allah and grounds it in His final judgment.
The next ayah turns the warning into a duty toward the nearest clan.
It repeats the prohibition on making another god with Allah and calls the speaker a clear warner.
It applies the same exclusive invocation rule to worship: call no one alongside Allah.
The promised divine bounty complements the prophetic warning only indirectly.
It repeats calling another god with Allah, denies its proof, and assigns the reckoning to the Lord.
It forbids calling what cannot benefit or harm besides Allah and names the act wrongdoing.
The immediate continuation joins the warning with humility toward those who follow in faith.
Naming Manat as another deity gives only a concrete but limited idolatry context.
The warning against denying Allah's signs adds a general loss consequence.

It closely repeats making another god with Allah and states the consequence of blame and rejection in Hell.
The immediate next step after care for followers is disavowal of the disobedient people's deeds.

It confirms the messenger's combined roles of witness, bearer of good news, and warner.
Allah's possession of the first and last supplies a broad final-accountability horizon.
The assertion of truth from the Lord does not develop invocation, warning, or punishment here.
The local sequence directs the messenger to rely on the Mighty, Merciful One after warning and response.

Fire as the recompense of wrongdoing gives a general punishment parallel.
It identifies the prophet as witness, bearer of good news, and warner, preparing the calling role in the next ayah.
Hell calling those who turned away presents punishment as the reversal of a refused call.
It combines warning, individual accountability, and the failure of even close kin to bear another's burden.

It contrasts Allah's kingdom with those invoked besides Him, who possess no power at all.
Jesus's signs repeatedly occur only by Allah's permission, giving a limited boundary against treating a messenger as independent.
Reminder for every returning servant relates only broadly to the warning's purpose.

Unrelieved punishment for a destructive exchange supplies only a general consequence.
The local conclusion names Allah as the All-Hearing, All-Knowing ground of the messenger's reliance and warning.
Noah's night-and-day call to his people gives a sustained prophetic-warning parallel.
It shows worldly possessions becoming a means of punishment for those who disbelieve.
Disbelievers' astonishment at a warner from among themselves parallels resistance to the warning mission.
Those formerly invoked besides Allah vanish, exposing their call as delusion before divine judgment.
Satan's final speech distinguishes his misleading call from Allah's true promise and ends in painful punishment.
The oath by the glorious Quran does not itself clarify the focus's invocation prohibition.

Answering the Lord is contrasted with a terrible reckoning and Hell for those who refuse.

The denial of being punished is the immediate contrary claim to the focus's explicit warning.
The messenger limits hidden knowledge to Allah while retaining his role as a clear warner.
Allah as the best of judges gives a broad basis for the threatened judgment.
The messenger must withdraw from those who mock Allah's signs, marking a response to hostile rejection.
Persistent disputation about Allah is set against His overwhelming power and possible punishment.
It directly asks whether they have any god other than Allah and rejects their association.
It declares that what is called besides Allah has no valid call in either world and leads to the Fire.
It makes the outcome of a warning known through impending punishment.
Calling Allah the God of humankind supplies a broad exclusive-worship title.
It joins personal responsibility with the rule that punishment follows the sending of a messenger.
It defines the prophet's office as warning in the face of demands for a sign.
It declares one God with no deity besides Him, but adds less than the earlier direct prohibitions.
It exposes taking religious authorities and the Messiah as lords besides Allah despite the command to worship one God.
Its call to peace is not an invocation or warning against association.
At punishment, repeated calls for destruction cannot repair the failed relationship of appeal.
The prescribed punishment gives only a general accountability parallel.
Allah alone has the call of truth; those invoked besides Him give no response.
The command to preserve named gods concretely displays the social maintenance of rival worship.
It qualifies the timing of divine punishment by the prophet's presence and people's seeking forgiveness.
Noah's call producing further flight illustrates rejection of a prophetic warning.
It affirms one God in heaven and earth, extending exclusive divinity across all domains.
Creation and provision culminate in the challenge, "Is there a god with Allah?"
Noah's public call supplies a clear prophetic-warning parallel.
The promised later resurrection supports the remote horizon of judgment.
Obedient companionship with prophets does not clarify rival invocation or its warning.
The condemned acknowledge that a warner came, then recall their denial of Allah's revelation.
Calling to good and forbidding evil is a broad communal analogue to warning.
Allah's greatest punishment is the stated consequence for turning away.
Noah's self-description as a clear warner parallels the prophetic office in the focus context.
Zechariah's prayer to his Lord shows direct prayer to the One who hears, but lacks the focus's polemic.
Physical nearness in a combat instruction does not illuminate the near-clan warning or exclusive invocation.

The small number of later people does not add to the focus's themes.
The Creator and Restorer challenges the claim that any god stands with Allah and demands proof.
People's obstinate refusal to hear Noah's call illustrates resistance to a warning meant for forgiveness.
Allah's exclusive deity is joined to the certain gathering for the Day of Resurrection.
The sacred-month regulation and combat command do not clarify the focus.
Evil punishment and ultimate loss give a general consequence for rejecting guidance.

It identifies Allah as the Truth and everything called besides Him as false.
Allah's oneness provides the basic monotheistic ground already made explicit by stronger cards.
Choosing Allah, His messenger, and the hereafter gives only an indirect orientation toward exclusive loyalty.
The lineage statement and divine hearing and knowledge do not clarify the focus.
Idols called toward guidance cannot respond, exposing their incapacity as objects of invocation.
Inheritance distribution does not add to the focus's warning against another deity.
Allah commands people to call on Him, promises response, and links refusal of worship to Hell.
The ruling on oaths and Allah's guardianship does not develop the focus's themes.
Allah's possession of both the hereafter and this life supplies a broad judgment horizon.
It commands worship of Allah alone and rejects taking lords beside Him.
It begins worship with Allah and directly prohibits associating anything with Him.
It names association with Allah as the decisive unforgiven wrong without repentance.
It repeats the gravity of associating partners with Allah and its departure from the right path.
It describes those who call on beings besides Allah, exposing the invoked alternative as a satanic allegiance.
It condemns deifying the Messiah and commands worship of Allah as the shared Lord.
It rejects the claim of multiple gods and warns its adherents of painful punishment.
It asks why anything that cannot harm or benefit should be worshipped besides Allah.
In distress people call Allah alone, and He removes the harm if He wills.
The messenger is expressly forbidden to worship those invoked besides Allah.
It portrays people calling Allah humbly in danger and promising gratitude upon rescue.
It asks whether people should call what neither benefits nor harms instead of Allah.
Abraham's question about taking idols as gods gives a direct prophetic challenge to rival worship.
It rebukes making the jinn partners with Allah despite His sole creative authority.
It declares Allah the Creator of all things and that there is no deity except Him.
It regulates engagement with those who call others besides Allah, acknowledging the social setting of rival worship.
It prohibits associating with Allah anything for which He gave no authority.
It depicts the failure of those invoked besides Allah when they are summoned for judgment.
Noah's call to worship Allah because there is no other god establishes the recurring warning formula.
Hud's people are commanded to worship Allah alone, directly linking monotheism and prophetic warning.
Salih's warning to worship Allah alone continues the same prophetic pattern.
Shuayb's command to worship Allah alone joins exclusive devotion to public reform.
It describes people assigning partners to Allah after receiving what He alone created.
Those invoked besides Allah are servants who cannot answer their callers.
The beings called besides Allah cannot help their worshippers or help themselves.
It rejects worshipping besides Allah what neither harms nor benefits and calls the claim of intercession false.
At sea in distress people call Allah sincerely, making exclusive invocation visible under pressure.
At judgment Allah separates the associators from their alleged partners and exposes their disavowal.
It challenges those who call alleged partners besides Allah as following conjecture rather than truth.
The messenger is told to worship Allah alone, the One who causes death.
It declares that there is no deity except Allah and makes surrender the proper response.
The gods called besides Allah bring their people no benefit when divine judgment arrives.
Joseph rejects associating anything with Allah as part of the inherited prophetic faith.
It contrasts many competing lords with Allah, the One and Overpowering.
It states that judgment belongs only to Allah and commands worship of Him alone.
It condemns setting equals to Allah that lead people away from His path.
Those invoked besides Allah create nothing and are themselves created.
It forbids taking two gods and declares that Allah is only one God.
It rejects worshipping besides Allah beings with no power over provision.
It challenges people to call those they claim besides Allah, who cannot remove or transfer harm.
Those called besides Allah themselves seek nearness to their Lord, so cannot be independent rivals.
When danger comes at sea, every invoked alternative disappears except Allah.
The companions refuse ever to call another god besides their Lord.
It rejects the people's gods besides Allah and demands proof for their claim.
Allah has no partner in judgment, strengthening the focus's exclusive divine authority.
Those claimed as Allah's partners are called but do not answer, and no saving bond is found.
Abraham warns his father not to worship Satan, identifying false worship as misplaced allegiance.
Abraham separates from his people's objects of invocation and calls on his Lord instead.
Allah declares that there is no god but Him and commands worship and remembrance directed to Him.
It identifies Allah alone as God, with no deity besides Him and all-encompassing knowledge.
It argues that multiple gods would corrupt heaven and earth, defending Allah's unique sovereignty.
It challenges the claim that gods exist besides Allah and demands its evidence.
Every messenger receives the same revelation: there is no god but Allah, so worship Him.
It asks whether alleged gods can protect people from Allah, exposing their inability to save.
Abraham asks why people worship besides Allah what neither benefits nor harms them.
It announces that the revealed God is one, placing the prophetic message under exclusive devotion.
It commands devotion to Allah without associating anything with Him and warns of the fall from that state.
Those called besides Allah cannot create even a fly, establishing their utter incapacity.
It denies that Allah has a child or that any god exists alongside Him.
It declares Allah the true King and that there is no deity except Him.
It describes alleged gods besides Allah as unable to create, benefit, harm, give death, or give life.
It rebukes worship of what cannot benefit or harm apart from Allah.
It clarifies that devils did not bring down the revelation immediately before the focus's warning.
It excludes devils from both the fitness and capacity to bear the revealed message.
It states that devils are barred from hearing, sharpening the divine source of the warning.
It turns from the divine warning to identify the kind of people upon whom devils descend.
It characterizes them as sinful liars, contrasting their source with the revealed warning.
It distinguishes poets followed by the erring from the messenger's divinely grounded warning.
It condemns saying what one does not do, a boundary for credible warning.
It preserves an exception for believers who do righteous deeds and remember Allah abundantly.
Abraham's question to his father and people, "What do you worship?", begins a direct inquiry into rival devotion.
Their answer that they remain devoted to idols supplies a concrete counterpart to the focus's prohibition.
Abraham tests whether the idols hear when called, directly interrogating their fitness as invoked beings.
He asks whether the idols benefit or harm, matching the Quranic test for false objects of invocation.
Abraham calls attention to the very objects worshipped by the people and their ancestors.
He declares all such objects enemies except the Lord of the worlds.
At judgment the question, "Where are what you used to worship?", carries rival worship into its final reckoning.
The question specifies that the missing objects were worshipped besides Allah.
The condemned acknowledge that their error was treating others as equal to the Lord of the worlds.
The Creator's ordering of earth, waters, and barriers culminates in the challenge, "Is there a god with Allah?"
Allah answers the distressed caller and removes harm, then asks whether any god is with Him.
Guidance through land and sea darkness is followed by the same challenge to any god with Allah.
Exclusive knowledge of the unseen belongs to Allah, limiting claims made for rivals.
The messenger is commanded to worship the Lord of the sacred city alone.
On judgment day Allah asks the associators where their claimed partners are.
They are told to call their partners, but the partners do not answer them.
It declares Allah alone God, with no deity except Him, and assigns all praise and judgment to Him.
It asks who other than Allah could bring light after an enduring night.
It asks who other than Allah could bring night for rest after an enduring day.
The repeated judgment question demands the location of the alleged partners.
It identifies worship besides Allah as devotion to idols and fabricated claims, while provision belongs to Allah.
Taking protectors besides Allah is compared to relying on a house too frail to sustain its inhabitants.
In danger at sea people call Allah sincerely, then revert to association after rescue.
Allah's parable rejects sharing His dominion with beings people themselves would not accept as equal partners.
It commands turning to Allah and explicitly forbids being among the associators.
It asks whether any alleged partners perform any part of Allah's creating, providing, causing death, or giving life.
Luqman's warning calls association with Allah a tremendous wrongdoing.
It commands calling those claimed besides Allah and states that they possess no weight of power anywhere.
Those called besides Allah neither hear the call nor can answer it, and will deny the association on judgment day.
It rejects taking gods besides Allah because their intercession cannot help against His intended harm.
It exposes the taking of gods besides Allah in hope of help.
It records arrogant refusal when people were told that there is no god but Allah.
Abraham asks his people what it is that they worship.
He rebukes worshipping what people themselves carve while Allah created them and their work.
Elijah's mission supplies another prophetic warning against false worship.
He asks why they call on Baal and abandon Allah, the best of creators.
The opponents are astonished that the messenger has made all gods one God.
The messenger declares that there is no deity except Allah, the One and Overpowering.
It commands sincere religion for Allah and rejects taking protectors besides Him.
Those who admit Allah created the heavens and earth are still challenged over what they call besides Him.
It questions taking intercessors besides Allah even when they possess nothing and understand nothing.
Mention of Allah alone provokes aversion in associators, revealing the resistance targeted by the focus.
The messenger rejects being commanded to worship other than Allah.
It explains punishment through rejecting belief when Allah alone was called upon and believing when partners were associated.
Allah judges in truth, while those called besides Him have no judgment power.
The believer rejects being called to associate with Allah what he has no knowledge of.
At judgment the associators are asked where their alleged partners are.
The messenger announces that the hearers' God is one and calls them to uprightness toward Him.
It forbids prostration to sun and moon and commands prostration to Allah who created them.
Allah watches over those who take protectors besides Him, while the messenger is not their keeper.
It contrasts other protectors with Allah, the true Protector who gives life to the dead.
It challenges alleged partners that prescribe religion without Allah's authorization.
Abraham disavows what his father and people worship, directing loyalty toward the Creator.
The messenger is told to ask whether any gods besides the Most Merciful were appointed for worship.
Jesus directs worship to Allah as his Lord and the people's Lord.
Taking desire as a god shows another form of transferring ultimate allegiance from Allah.
It demands evidence for those called besides Allah by asking what they created or share in.
It calls no one more astray than one who invokes besides Allah beings unable to answer until resurrection.
At the gathering, the invoked beings become enemies and reject the worship directed to them.
The alleged gods taken for nearness do not help when judgment comes and vanish as fabricated claims.
Knowledge that there is no deity except Allah grounds the messenger's call in explicit monotheism.
The named goddesses provide a concrete catalogue of the rivals opposed by the focus.
Their authority is reduced to names and conjecture rather than revealed proof.
Allah's exalted majesty excludes the familial and dependent claims associated with rival worship.
The messenger declares that he calls only upon his Lord and associates no one with Him.
He denies possessing independent power to harm or guide, keeping divine power from being divided.
